character_and_relationship_context: Tyler Hoffman is a twenty-two-year-old from a suburb outside Columbus, Ohio. He grew up in a split-level house with a backyard that always had a half-finished deck project, his dad's tools scattered on the patio. His mother works as a dental hygienist, his father as a sales rep for an industrial supply company. They paid for his community college tuition without complaint, and they still cover his car insurance and phone plan, which he treats as a background fact of life rather than a gift that requires gratitude. He has a way of leaning back in his chair and stretching his arms over his head when he talks about what he's planning next, like he's already moving on from the conversation. That gesture carries over to how he handles commitments: he signed up for a CNA class last fall, then dropped it after three weeks because the textbook diagrams made him feel like he was back in high school biology, which he'd slept through. He dropped out of his computer science program this past spring, not because he failed but because he found himself spending more time scrolling through forums about other people's projects than actually writing code. The decision felt sudden to his professors, but Tyler had been mentally checking out for months. He took the overnight home-care job on a whim when his friend Jake backed out and asked him to fill in for one shift. Tyler ended up staying because he discovered he liked the quiet of third shift—the way the house settles, the slow repetition of checking vitals and repositioning the client. He works for a disabled veteran named Roy, a man in his sixties who needs help with transfers and medication but is still sharp and dry-humored. Tyler has already rearranged his shift schedule twice to start a weekend phlebotomy certificate program at a local vocational center. He tells people it's because he wants to do something real, something with his hands, but he also mentions that the phlebotomy instructor has a reputation for being strict, and Tyler thinks that might be good for him. He's not sure. He has a habit of picking up small notebooks and filling them with lists—certification deadlines, shift trade requests, possible jobs—then leaving them in the glovebox or on the kitchen counter, half-used. His parents' comfortable middle-class cushion means he never has to follow through on anything he starts, and he knows this. He sometimes brings it up himself, saying, 'I know I'm privileged,' but he says it in a way that acknowledges the problem without actually changing his pattern. There's a tension there: he genuinely admires people who stick with things, like his father, who has worked the same sales territory for twenty years, and Roy, who still does his daily exercises without anyone watching. Tyler has started to notice that he respects those people more than himself, but he hasn't figured out what to do with that feeling. His culture is Midwestern in the practical sense—weather talk, potluck dinners, a general avoidance of direct emotional confrontation. He grew up in a house where his parents expressed love through paying for things and leaving decaf coffee in the pot for the morning, not through long talks. That's shaped how he approaches Roy: he shows up on time, does the work, and doesn't pry into Roy's wartime stories unless Roy brings them up. He's learning that caring for someone is less about decoding feelings and more about the rhythm of nights—the beep of the monitor, the creak of the stair, the way Roy's hand grips the walker at exactly the right moment. Tyler doesn't know if he'll finish the phlebotomy program. He's curious to see if he can. His dad leaves decisions open-ended, so Tyler carries the guilt of skipping himself. His mom files away absences and may mention them offhand later. John and the Millers have known Tyler since childhood and always ask what he's 'doing now,' which he finds gently uncomfortable. When a new program starts, Tyler treats it as urgent and reschedules social plans around it for the first month. At past watch parties he arrived near kickoff and never missed one entirely, though he drifted to the porch by the second quarter. He has texted his family to back out of plans before, citing homework or errands, and they accepted it without pushback.
objective_situation: On a September Saturday, Tyler's dad calls to say the neighbors are gathering at the house for the Ohio State game. He mentions that John is bringing chili and the Millers are bringing meatballs, then adds, 'Grab a twelve-pack or a bag of chips if you want.' Tyler had planned to spend the afternoon reviewing the phlebotomy course schedule online and running errands. He knows these watch parties have unwritten rules around kickoff: show up before the game starts, make small talk during commercials, bring something to contribute, and don't slip out early. Empty-handed guests are noticed in his parents' neighborhood, and so is obvious disinterest in the game.
state_and_available_memories: He's a few weeks into the phlebotomy program, unsure whether weekend classes will stick while he works third shift. He's running short on sleep from the week's overnights. His errands include picking up the course textbook. The offer of a twelve-pack or chips pulls up last year's party, when he arrived with pretzels and his mom handed him the chip bowl so he'd look prepared. 'Kickoff' recalls his dad's rule that no one answers their phone during the first half. He remembers his dad driving him to community college without mentioning cost — just dropping him off, his family's way of showing support. He also felt easiest at a small Sunday dinner with only his parents, no neighbors asking what he was doing next.
name: Tyler Hoffman
